## <mark>ERYTHROPLASIA OF QUEYRAT</mark>

### <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>

<mark>Erythroplasia of Queyrat (EQ) is an in situ squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) that affects the mucosal surfaces of the penis in uncircumcised males.</mark> First described by Queyrat in 1911 as "erythroplasie du gland," the term *erythroplasia of Queyrat* is preferred over SCC in situ or Bowen disease (BD) due to its distinct clinical presentation—typically a well-demarcated, shiny, velvety, bright red plaque.

<mark>EQ occurs in uncircumcised men aged 20 to 80 years, with most cases occurring between the third and sixth decades of life.</mark> <mark>Risk factors include poor genital hygiene, smegma accumulation, heat, friction, trauma, and genital herpes simplex virus infection.</mark> 

Human papillomavirus (HPV) plays a significant role in pathogenesis. <mark>Co-infection with HPV subtypes 8 and 16 has been identified in nearly all studied EQ lesions.</mark> <mark>Additional involvement of high-risk subtypes such as HPV-39 and/or HPV-51 has also been observed.</mark> <mark>This dual or multiple HPV infection pattern may distinguish EQ from BD and other genital neoplasias, suggesting a unique virological etiology.</mark>

---

### AT A GLANCE

- <mark>Erythroplasia of Queyrat (EQ) is an in situ SCC of the penile mucosa in uncircumcised males.</mark>  
- <mark>Clinically distinct from Bowen disease.</mark>  
- <mark>Associated with HPV types 8 and 16 in most cases.</mark>  
- <mark>Progresses to invasive SCC in approximately 10% of untreated cases.</mark>  
- Preventive measures include circumcision and good genital hygiene.  
- First-line treatment: **Mohs micrographic surgery**.  
- Alternative treatments: Surgical excision, $\mathrm{CO}_2$ laser vaporization, and topical 5-fluorouracil.

---

### Clinical Findings

<mark>EQ typically presents as a glistening, red, velvety plaque on the glans penis, prepuce, or urethral meatus.</mark> <mark>About 50% of cases begin as a solitary lesion, while the rest present with multiple plaques.</mark> 

Common symptoms include:
- Localized pain
- Pruritus
- Phimosis (difficulty retracting the foreskin)
- Bleeding
- Crusting

These clinical features overlap with other penile conditions, necessitating biopsy for definitive diagnosis.

---

### Histopathology

<mark>Histologically, EQ resembles Bowen disease, showing full-thickness epidermal atypia with preserved tissue architecture.</mark> However, distinguishing features may include:
- Epidermal hypoplasia (thinning)
- Prominent dermal plasma cell infiltrate—commonly seen in mucosal inflammatory and neoplastic conditions

These histologic nuances support the diagnosis when correlated clinically.

---

### Diagnosis and Differential Diagnosis

The differential diagnosis includes:
- Psoriasis
- Seborrheic dermatitis
- Lichen planus
- Lichen sclerosus
- Candidiasis
- Plasma cell balanitis (Zoon balanitis)
- Lymphogranuloma venereum
- Granuloma inguinale
- Syphilis
- Drug eruptions

<mark>Given the broad differential, **a biopsy is essential** whenever EQ is suspected to confirm the diagnosis and rule out mimickers.</mark>

---

### Prognosis and Clinical Course

EQ lesions tend to persist and slowly enlarge, often present for several years—average duration of 3.4 years before diagnosis in one study—before medical evaluation and biopsy. 

Compared to Bowen disease, EQ has a higher risk of progression to invasive squamous cell carcinoma, estimated at **approximately 10% of cases**. Early diagnosis and appropriate treatment are crucial to prevent malignant transformation and complications.

# <mark>Bowenoid Papulosis, Bowen's Disease of the Penis, and Erythroplasia of Queyrat</mark>

The terms **Bowenoid papulosis**, **Bowen's disease of the penis**, and **Erythroplasia of Queyrat** remain clinically useful. <mark>They describe distinct clinical presentations and reflect a spectrum of penile intraepithelial neoplasia (PeIN) with varying risks of progression to **squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)**.</mark> <mark>While all may progress to invasive SCC, the risk differs significantly:</mark>

- <mark>**Bowenoid papulosis**: ~1% risk of progression</mark>  
- <mark>**Bowen's disease of the penis**: ~5% risk</mark>  
- <mark>**Erythroplasia of Queyrat**: 10%–40% risk</mark>  

<mark>These entities represent different phenotypes within the broader category of PeIN.</mark>

---

## <mark>PeIN of the Balanopreputial Epithelium (Erythroplasia of Queyrat)</mark>

- <mark>**Typical appearance**: Red, velvety, well-circumscribed lesion on the glans or inner prepuce, typically in uncircumcised men.</mark>

---

## <mark>PeIN of Keratinized, Hair-Bearing Skin (Bowen's Disease of the Penis)</mark>

- <mark>**Typical appearance**: Scaly, discrete, erythematous patches or plaques on the shaft skin.</mark>

---

## <mark>PeIN (Bowenoid Papulosis)</mark>

- <mark>**Typical appearance**: Clinically resembles genital warts; lesions may be pigmented or erythematous papules or plaques, often grouped.</mark>  
- <mark>**Patient profile**: Typically younger individuals compared to those with Bowen’s disease or Erythroplasia of Queyrat.</mark>

---

## <mark>Diagnosis</mark>

- <mark>**Biopsy is essential**</mark>  
- <mark>Histology reveals **penile intraepithelial neoplasia**, which can be:</mark>
  <mark>- **Differentiated type**: Associated with lichen sclerosus</mark>  
  <mark>- **Undifferentiated type**: HPV-associated</mark>

---

## Management

<mark>Patients with suspected penile cancer or precancer should be managed jointly by **dermatology and urology/andrology** specialists.</mark> <mark>A combined, sequential approach is often required, tailored to:</mark>

- <mark>Patient age, comorbidities, and immunosuppression status (e.g., HIV, transplant recipients)</mark>  
- <mark>Anatomical site(s) involved</mark>  
- <mark>Circumcision status</mark>  
- <mark>Underlying pathogenesis (HPV vs. lichen sclerosus)</mark>  
- <mark>Histological subtype (differentiated vs. undifferentiated)</mark>

### Topical Medical Therapies

- **Imiquimod 5%** (Evidence level: 1,C)  
- **Fluorouracil cream 5%** (2,C)  
- **Fluorouracil 0.5% / salicylic acid 10% combination** (2,C)

### Surgical and Ablative Treatments (aim for tissue conservation)

- **Surgical excision** – Local excision usually sufficient and effective (1,B)  
- **Mohs micrographic surgery** (1,B)  
- **Cryotherapy** (2,D)  
- **Photodynamic therapy** (2,D)  
- **Laser ablation** (2,D)  
- **Mandatory circumcision** for balanopreputial disease, especially in high-risk patients (e.g., HIV, transplant recipients) (1,D)  
- **Glans resurfacing** – Considered if topical treatments fail (2,D)

### Adjunctive Measures

- **Polyvalent HPV vaccination** (2,D)  
- **Smoking cessation** (2,D)

---

## Follow-up

- **Follow-up is usually mandatory** due to risks of field cancerization and recurrence. Up to one-third of patients may have microinvasive or invasive disease at presentation.  
- The optimal duration of follow-up is uncertain.  
- **Circumcised patients with Bowenoid papulosis or PeIN confined to the prepuce** may be considered for discharge after successful treatment.  
- **Circumcision is strongly recommended** in relevant cases due to the risk of progression and recurrence.

## Hyperpigmentation in Thyrotoxicosis

The occurrence of hyperpigmentation in thyrotoxic patients has been estimated to range from 2 percent to as high as 40 percent in large series. <mark>The increased cutaneous pigmentation can be localized or generalized and is more common in individuals with darker skin.</mark> The distribution often resembles that seen in Addison disease, with pigment deposition in the creases of the palms and soles. However, several distinguishing features exist: mucous membrane involvement is uncommon, and pigmentation of the nipples and genital skin is less pronounced.

Hyperpigmentation associated with thyrotoxicosis is thought to result from increased release of pituitary ACTH, which compensates for accelerated cortisol degradation. The response of hyperpigmentation to treatment for hyperthyroidism is generally poor. Autoimmune Graves disease has also been reported in association with vitiligo.

## <mark>Melasma</mark>

<mark>Melasma is a common hypermelanosis that typically affects sun-exposed areas of the face.</mark> <mark>Its pathogenesis is not fully understood, but genetic and hormonal factors, in combination with UV radiation, play important roles.</mark> <mark>Specific precipitating factors include:</mark>

- <mark>Oral contraceptives</mark>  
- <mark>Estrogen replacement therapy</mark>  
- <mark>Mild ovarian or thyroid dysfunction</mark>  
- <mark>Ovarian tumors</mark>  
- <mark>Cosmetics</mark>  
- <mark>Nutritional factors</mark>  
- <mark>Phototoxic and photoallergic medications</mark>  
- <mark>Antiepileptic drugs</mark>  

<mark>Melasma is rarely reported before puberty and is significantly more common in women, especially those of reproductive age.</mark> <mark>Individuals with darker skin types (Fitzpatrick types IV, V, or VI) are more frequently affected.</mark>

<mark>Lesions appear as brownish macules with irregular borders and a symmetric facial distribution, often coalescing into a reticular pattern.</mark> <mark>Sun exposure exacerbates the condition.</mark> <mark>Three major patterns of distribution are recognized:</mark>

- <mark>**Centrofacial (63%)**: forehead, nose, chin, and upper lip</mark>  
- <mark>**Malar (21%)**: cheeks and nose</mark>  
- <mark>**Mandibular (16%)**: ramus of the mandible</mark>  

<mark>The anterior chest and dorsal forearms may also be involved.</mark>

<mark>Under Wood's lamp examination, melasma is classically categorized as epidermal, dermal, or mixed.</mark> <mark>The epidermal type shows sharp borders and enhanced visibility under Wood's lamp, while the dermal or mixed type appears blotchy and is less apparent.</mark> <mark>In most cases, melanin is distributed in the basal layer of the epidermis and the dermis.</mark>

<mark>Sun exposure is a major contributing factor, and sun protection is essential in management.</mark> <mark>Epidermal pigmentation tends to respond better to topical treatments than dermal pigmentation.</mark> <mark>Effective hypopigmenting agents include:</mark>

- <mark>Hydroquinone</mark>  
- <mark>Tretinoin cream</mark>  
- <mark>Azelaic acid</mark>  
- Rucinol  
- <mark>Kojic acid</mark>  

<mark>The Kligman formula—a combination of hydroquinone, tretinoin, and a weak topical corticosteroid—is widely used.</mark> <mark>Chemical peels and laser therapy may be beneficial but carry a risk of inducing further hyperpigmentation.</mark> <mark>In some cases, melasma gradually resolves after withdrawal of hormonal triggers and with strict sun avoidance.</mark>

## Pigmentation Changes in Pregnancy

During pregnancy, increased pigmentation occurs in approximately 90% of women and is more pronounced in those with darker skin types. Pre-existing pigmented lesions such as nevi and ephelides often darken, and recent scars may also become hyperpigmented. Normally pigmented areas—including the nipples, areolae, and genitalia—typically exhibit intensified coloration.

The linea alba, the midline of the anterior abdominal wall, frequently becomes hyperpigmented during pregnancy and is then referred to as **linea nigra**. A small proportion of pregnant women develop hyperpigmentation in the axillae or inner upper thighs.

Melasma, commonly known as the "mask of pregnancy," affects more than 50% of pregnant women.

## Acanthosis Nigricans

Acanthosis nigricans is a condition characterized by hyperpigmentation and velvety thickening of the skin, typically in intertriginous areas. It is associated with insulin resistance, obesity, and endocrinopathies, and is discussed in detail in Chapters 152 and 154.

## Diabetes and Skin Pigmentation

(See Chapter on Diabetes)

## Hyperpigmentation in Various Conditions

Pre-existing pigmented lesions such as **nevi** and **ephelides** become darker during pregnancy. Also, recent scars often darken. In normally pigmented areas such as the **nipples**, **areolae**, and **genitalia**, the pigmentation becomes more intense. The **linea alba**, the median line on the anterior abdominal wall, often becomes hyperpigmented during pregnancy and is then called **linea nigra**. In a small proportion of pregnant women, hyperpigmentation occurs in the **axillae** or the **inner upper thighs**. <mark>**Melasma**, or "mask of pregnancy" (see the section Melasma), occurs in more than 50 percent of pregnant women (see Chap.</mark> 107).

### Acanthosis Nigricans
**Acanthosis nigricans** is associated with hyperpigmentation and is discussed in Chaps. 152 and 154.

### Diabetes
(See Chap. 153) A higher **vitiligo** prevalence has been reported in patients with **diabetes type I and II** compared to the general population. **Diabetic dermopathy** is characterized by asymptomatic, irregular, light brown, depressed patches on the anterior lower legs, but the pathogenesis is not known.

### Nutritional Conditions
(See Chap. 130) Pigmentary changes can be secondary to nutritional conditions such as **kwashiorkor**, **vitamin B₁₂ deficiency**, **folic acid deficiency**, or **pellagra**. The skin changes are reversible upon correction of the nutritional deficiency.

### <mark>Metabolic Conditions</mark>

#### Porphyria Cutanea Tarda
<mark>**Porphyria cutanea tarda** is a metabolic disorder associated with diffuse brown hypermelanosis, accentuated in sun-exposed areas.</mark> <mark>In females, a melasma-like facial hyperpigmentation can be observed (see Chap.</mark> 132).

#### Hemochromatosis
**Hereditary hemochromatosis** is an autosomal recessive disorder associated with increased intestinal absorption of iron and deposition of excessive iron in the liver, pancreas, and other organs, including the skin. In the past, hemochromatosis was typically diagnosed at an advanced stage by the classic triad of **hyperpigmentation**, **diabetes mellitus** ("bronze diabetes"), and **hepatic cirrhosis**. Skin darkening was present in 70% of patients, due to two mechanisms:  
- **Hemosiderin deposition**, causing a diffuse slate-gray discoloration  
- **Increased melanin production**, causing a bronze hue  

Because hemochromatosis is now usually diagnosed earlier, hyperpigmentation is less frequently observed. The pigmentation is typically generalized but may be more pronounced in sun-exposed areas, genitalia, and scars. <mark>Skin bronzing is reversible once phlebotomy therapy is initiated.</mark>

### Tumoral Conditions

#### Mast Cell Disorders
Mast cell disorders can lead to hyperpigmentation and are discussed in Chap. 150.

#### Melanoma
(See Chap. 124) **Diffuse generalized melanosis** associated with advanced metastatic melanoma is a rare but well-documented event. It is characterized by a slate bluish-gray to brown discoloration of the skin. Histology reveals melanin particles and melanin-containing histiocytes and dendritic cells in the dermis and subcutaneous fat. No melanoma cells are detected in the skin, and there is no increase in epidermal melanin or melanocyte number. Circulating melanosomes have been detected in the blood, supporting the hypothesis that diffuse melanosis may result from tumor lysis with release of melanosomes into the circulation and subsequent deposition in the skin.

### Physical Agents

#### Ultraviolet Radiation
The major acute effects of UV radiation on normal human skin are **sunburn**, followed by **tanning** (see Chap. 89).

#### Ionizing Radiation
(See Chap. 95) Exposure of the skin to ionizing radiation—such as in nuclear accidents (e.g., Chernobyl) or after local fractionated radiotherapy—can lead to **cutaneous radiation syndrome**, characterized by fibrosis, keratosis, telangiectasias, and sharply demarcated lentiginous hyperpigmentation resembling UV-induced lentigines.

# CUTANEOUS CHANGES COMMONLY ASSOCIATED WITH PREGNANCY

## AT A GLANCE

<mark>Cutaneous changes result from the altered endocrine, metabolic, and immunologic milieu that characterize pregnancy.</mark>  
<mark>Pigmentary disturbances, including hyperpigmentation, darkening of the linea alba, and melasma are the changes most commonly observed.</mark>  
Significant change in nevi size is not a feature of most pregnancies.  
Structural changes known to occur during pregnancy include, most commonly, striae distensae.  
Pruritus is a common complaint during pregnancy and may be related to flare of a pre-existing dermatosis or onset of a specific dermatosis of pregnancy.

---

## <mark>Melasma (Chloasma)</mark>

<mark>Melasma or chloasma is a common finding characterized by irregular, blotchy facial hyperpigmentation that occurs in up to 70 percent of pregnant women.</mark> <mark>This condition is exacerbated by sun exposure and oral contraceptive use in nonpregnant women.</mark> <mark>Melasma may regress postpartum, but it often persists, posing a therapeutic challenge.</mark>

## Changes in Melanocytic Nevi

Historically, changes in melanocytic nevi have been considered normal during pregnancy. However, objective data are limited. Pennoyer et al. photographically monitored 129 melanocytic nevi in 22 healthy Caucasian women throughout pregnancy. Only eight nevi (6.2 percent) showed changes in diameter between the first and third trimesters, with a mean size change of zero. The study concluded that significant change in nevus size—excluding nevi on the abdominal skin stretched by pregnancy—does not typically occur during gestation. Therefore, any pigmented lesion in a pregnant woman that changes in morphology (size, color, or shape) or develops symptoms (such as itching, bleeding, or scaling) should be considered for histopathologic evaluation.

## Striae Distensae (Striae Gravidarum)

Striae distensae, commonly known as stretch marks, are the most frequent structural skin change during pregnancy. They typically appear on areas prone to stretching, including the abdomen, hips, buttocks, and breasts. Genetic factors—such as family history, personal history, and race—are the strongest predictors of striae development, outweighing factors like pregnancy weight gain or changes in body mass index. These findings suggest a strong genetic predisposition to this condition.

## Pruritus in Pregnancy

Pruritus is a common symptom during pregnancy. It may be physiologic or may indicate a flare of a pre-existing skin condition (e.g., atopic dermatitis) or the onset of a pregnancy-specific dermatosis. Most pregnant patients with pruritic skin disease have conditions unrelated to pregnancy. However, a smaller subset develops dermatoses specific to pregnancy, some of which are associated with fetal risk.

---

# DERMATOSES ASSOCIATED WITH FETAL RISK IN PREGNANCY

## Pemphigoid Gestationis (Herpes Gestationis)

Pemphigoid gestationis (PG) is an intensely pruritic, vesiculobullous eruption that typically occurs in mid to late pregnancy or the immediate postpartum period. It classically presents during the second or third trimester with the sudden onset of severely itchy urticarial lesions on normal or erythematous skin.

## <mark>Definition and Pathogenesis of Atopy</mark>

<mark>Atopy can be defined as a familial hypersensitivity of the skin and mucosa to environmental substances, associated with increased production of immunoglobulin E (IgE) or altered pharmacologic reactivity.</mark> <mark>The ETFAD defines atopy as the "familial tendency to develop Th2 responses against common environmental antigens," encompassing both IgE-associated (extrinsic) and non-IgE-associated (intrinsic) subtypes within the atopic spectrum.</mark>

## Genetic and Molecular Basis

Atopic diseases are genetically linked, with a concordance rate of 80% in monozygotic twins compared to 30% in dizygotic twins. Genetic polymorphisms involved in atopic dermatitis (AD) affect mediators of atopic inflammation located on various chromosomes, some of which are also implicated in respiratory atopy. The strongest genetic association is with mutations in the *filaggrin* gene, which is also linked to ichthyosis vulgaris, underscoring the role of epidermal barrier dysfunction in AD. Clinically, concomitant ichthyosis vulgaris may be identified by increased palmar hyperlinearity, a useful indicator of filaggrin gene mutations.

## <mark>Clinical Presentation</mark>

In early infancy, AD may present as "cradle cap"—a yellowish, seborrheic, crusted scaling on the scalp—which typically responds to emollient therapy alone. <mark>The disease usually begins on the face (with relative sparing of the middle face), extensor surfaces of the limbs, and trunk, often with oozing and crusting.</mark> <mark>As the child grows, involvement shifts to the flexural areas, neck, and hands, accompanied by dry skin.</mark>

Skin barrier dysfunction in AD is evidenced by increased transepidermal water loss (TEWL). Measuring TEWL with an evaporimeter and discussing results with patients can enhance adherence to emollient therapy. Lichenification results from chronic scratching and rubbing, often occurring at night. The prurigo variant of AD is characterized by excoriated, nodular, and lichenified lesions.

Exacerbations typically begin with intense pruritus in the absence of visible lesions, followed by erythema, papules, and infiltration. Histopathologic findings are not specific for AD; thus, routine biopsy is not diagnostic but may help exclude conditions such as cutaneous T-cell lymphoma in adults.

## <mark>Diagnosis</mark>

<mark>In the absence of a specific laboratory marker, AD is diagnosed clinically.</mark> <mark>While an experienced clinician’s judgment surpasses available diagnostic criteria, standardized criteria are essential for epidemiological studies and clinical trial enrollment.</mark> <mark>Most criteria focus on cutaneous signs of atopy.</mark>

- <mark>**Hanifin and Rajka criteria** require three of the following four: pruritus, typical morphology and distribution, chronic or relapsing course, and personal or family history of atopy. Additionally, at least three minor criteria from a list of 21 must be fulfilled.</mark>
- <mark>**UK Working Party criteria** include an itchy skin condition in the past 12 months plus at least three of the following: onset before age two, history of skin fold involvement, generalized dry skin, personal or family history of other atopic diseases, and visible flexural eczema.</mark>

## Impact on Quality of Life

Atopic dermatitis significantly affects all aspects of a patient’s life. Moderate-to-severe AD is associated with depression, anxiety, reduced quality of life, impaired self-esteem, and increased suicide risk. The social burden of moderate-to-severe AD is comparable to that of psoriasis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cardiovascular disease, and diabetes.

## Management of Flares

Managing acute exacerbations (flares) of AD is challenging, requiring rapid symptom control without disrupting long-term management goals such as flare prevention and minimizing treatment side effects. Flares may reveal underlying triggers, including allergies or infections. Therefore, initial evaluation should include a detailed history of flare circumstances and a thorough dermatologic examination, including assessment of lymph nodes, orifices, and skin folds. A professional and empathetic approach during flare management lays the foundation for future treatment adherence.

# POSITION STATEMENT

## <mark>ETFAD/EADV Eczema Task Force 2020 Position Paper on Diagnosis and Treatment of Atopic Dermatitis in Adults and Children</mark>

### Abstract

<mark>**Atopic dermatitis (AD)** is a highly pruritic, chronic inflammatory skin disease.</mark> <mark>The diagnosis is made using established clinical criteria.</mark> <mark>Disease activity and burden are best assessed with a composite score that evaluates both objective and subjective symptoms, such as the **SCORing Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD)** index.</mark>

<mark>Management of AD must consider clinical and pathogenic variability, the patient’s age, and the goal of flare prevention.</mark> <mark>**Basic therapy** includes universal application of hydrating and barrier-stabilizing topical treatments, as well as avoidance of specific and non-specific triggering factors.</mark>

<mark>Visible skin lesions are treated with **anti-inflammatory topical agents**, including **corticosteroids** and **calcineurin inhibitors** (tacrolimus and pimecrolimus), the latter being preferred for sensitive areas such as the face and folds.</mark> <mark>**Topical tacrolimus** and certain mid-potency corticosteroids are evidence-based options for **proactive therapy**—defined as long-term, intermittent anti-inflammatory treatment of areas prone to frequent relapses.</mark>

<mark>**Systemic anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive treatments** are evolving rapidly and require careful monitoring.</mark> <mark>**Oral corticosteroids** have a largely unfavourable benefit-risk profile and should be avoided when possible.</mark> <mark>The **IL-4Rα blocker dupilumab** is a safe, effective, and licensed, though expensive, treatment option, with potential ocular side effects.</mark> <mark>Other emerging therapies include **biologics** targeting key pathways in the atopic immune response and various **Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors**.</mark>

<mark>**Dysbiosis** and skin infections can trigger disease exacerbations and may warrant adjunctive antimicrobial therapy.</mark> <mark>**Systemic antihistamines (H1-receptor blockers)** have limited efficacy in reducing AD-related itch and skin lesions.</mark>

<mark>**Adjuvant therapies** include **phototherapy**, preferably **narrowband UVB** or **UVA1**.</mark> <mark>**Coal tar** may be beneficial in atopic hand and foot eczema.</mark> <mark>**Dietary recommendations** should be individualized; elimination diets should only be implemented in cases of confirmed food allergy.</mark> <mark>**Allergen-specific immunotherapy** for aeroallergens may be considered in selected patients.</mark> <mark>**Psychosomatic counselling** is recommended to manage stress-induced flares.</mark>

<mark>Evidence-based **‘Eczema school’ educational programmes** and **therapeutic patient education** are strongly recommended for both children and adults.</mark>

---

### <mark>Introduction and Definitions</mark>

<mark>**Atopic dermatitis (AD)**, also known as atopic eczema, eczema, or neurodermitis, is an inflammatory, chronically relapsing, and intensely pruritic skin disorder that frequently occurs in families with a history of atopic diseases—such as AD, food allergy, bronchial asthma, or allergic rhinoconjunctivitis.</mark>

<mark>Current understanding positions AD as a **systemic Th2-driven disease**, with a high prevalence of atopic comorbidities, particularly in patients with moderate-to-severe disease.</mark> <mark>From a clinical and histopathological perspective, AD is characterized by **eosinophilic and spongiotic skin inflammation**, with distinct, age-dependent patterns in lesion distribution and morphology.</mark>

<mark>AD affects **2–10% of young adults** and up to **20% of children**, making it one of the most prevalent skin conditions worldwide.</mark> <mark>The diversity in proposed aetiological mechanisms is reflected in the various historical and regional terms used, including *neurodermitis* and *endogenous/constitutional eczema*.</mark>

<mark>**Atopy** is defined as a familial tendency toward hypersensitivity of the skin and mucosa to environmental antigens, typically associated with elevated **immunoglobulin E (IgE)** levels or altered pharmacological reactivity.</mark> <mark>The **ETFAD** defines atopy as the *"familial tendency to develop Th2 responses against common environmental antigens"*, encompassing both **IgE-mediated (extrinsic)** and **non-IgE-mediated (intrinsic)** subtypes of AD.</mark>

<mark>Atopic diseases are genetically linked, with a **concordance rate of 80% in monozygotic twins** compared to **30% in dizygotic twins**.</mark> <mark>Genetic polymorphisms associated with AD involve mediators of atopic inflammation across multiple chromosomes, some of which are also implicated in respiratory atopy.</mark>

# <mark>ATOPIC DERMATITIS</mark>

## <mark>AT A GLANCE</mark>

- Prevalence peak of 15% to 20% in early childhood in industrialized countries  
- <mark>Chronic or chronically relapsing inflammatory skin disorder characterized by:</mark>

  <mark>- **Pruritus**</mark>  
  <mark>- **Eczematous dermatitis** (acute, subacute, or chronic) with typical morphology and age-specific patterns</mark>  
    <mark>- Facial and extensor involvement in infancy</mark>  
    <mark>- Flexural eczema and lichenification in children and adults</mark>  

- <mark>Commonly associated with:</mark>  
  <mark>- Personal or family history of atopy (asthma, allergic rhinitis, atopic dermatitis)</mark>  
  <mark>- **Xerosis** and skin barrier dysfunction</mark>  
  <mark>- **Immunoglobulin E (IgE) reactivity**</mark>

- <mark>Multifactorial etiology involving genetic predisposition, environmental influences, immune dysregulation, and skin barrier defects</mark>  
- <mark>Associated alterations in T-cell responses, antigen processing, inflammatory cytokines, host defense proteins, allergen sensitivity, and susceptibility to infection</mark>

---

## ETIOLOGY AND PATHOGENESIS

<mark>Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a highly pruritic inflammatory skin disease resulting from complex interactions between:</mark>

- <mark>**Genetic susceptibility** leading to defective skin barrier function</mark>  
- <mark>**Dysregulation of the innate and adaptive immune systems**</mark>  
- <mark>**Environmental triggers**</mark>

### Risk Factors and the Hygiene Hypothesis

The rise in atopic diseases has been linked to aspects of the so-called "Western lifestyle," including:

- <mark>Small family size</mark>  
- <mark>Higher income and education levels (in both white and Black populations)</mark>  
- <mark>Migration from rural to urban environments</mark>  
- <mark>Increased use of antibiotics</mark>  

<mark>These factors have contributed to the **hygiene hypothesis**, which proposes that reduced exposure to infectious agents in early childhood—particularly through unhygienic contact with older siblings—may impair immune system development and increase susceptibility to allergic diseases.</mark>

---

## <mark>Decreased Skin Barrier Function</mark>

<mark>AD is associated with significant impairment of the epidermal barrier due to:</mark>

- <mark>Downregulation of **cornified envelope genes** (e.g., *filaggrin*, *loricrin*)</mark>  
- <mark>Reduced **ceramide levels** in the stratum corneum</mark>  
- <mark>Increased activity of **endogenous proteolytic enzymes**</mark>  
- <mark>Enhanced **trans-epidermal water loss (TEWL)**</mark>

<mark>External factors exacerbate barrier dysfunction:</mark>

- <mark>**Soaps and detergents** increase skin pH, activating endogenous proteases and further degrading the barrier</mark>  
- <mark>**Exogenous proteases** from *Staphylococcus aureus* and house dust mites can damage the epidermis</mark>  
- <mark>Atopic skin lacks sufficient **endogenous protease inhibitors**, worsening the imbalance</mark>

<mark>These abnormalities promote:</mark>

- <mark>Increased penetration of allergens through the skin</mark>  
- <mark>Enhanced microbial colonization (especially by *S. aureus*)</mark>  
- <mark>**Epicutaneous sensitization** to allergens, which may lead to stronger allergic immune responses compared to systemic or airway exposure</mark>  
- <mark>Potential predisposition to respiratory allergies later in life</mark>

---

## Immunopathology of Atopic Dermatitis

### <mark>Skin Immune Environment</mark>

- <mark>**Clinically unaffected skin** in AD patients shows:</mark>
  <mark>- Mild epidermal hyperplasia</mark>  
  <mark>- Sparse perivascular T-cell infiltrate</mark>  

- <mark>**Acute lesions** are marked by:</mark>

## <mark>Diagnosis and Differentiation</mark>

<mark>Each of these conditions can be differentiated by appropriate porphyrin studies.</mark> <mark>Careful evaluation of urine, stool, and plasma porphyrins will almost always permit confirmation of the diagnosis of **porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT)**.</mark> Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, such as naproxen, and antibiotics, such as tetracyclines and nalidixic acid, as well as a variety of other agents, may rarely produce bullous lesions closely resembling PCT; however, in contrast to true PCT, these cases show no evidence of abnormal porphyrins (see **pseudoporphyria**).

## Treatment

### <mark>General Approach</mark>
Initially, a careful history should be taken to identify potential environmental triggers (e.g., alcohol, estrogen, or chlorinated hydrocarbons) that may have induced the disease. If **HCV** or **HIV** infection is present, these should be managed appropriately. Elimination of the triggering agent alone may lead to gradual improvement. However, in most patients with PCT, more aggressive treatment is usually warranted to accelerate therapeutic benefit. Current treatment options include repeated **phlebotomy**, oral administration of **antimalarials** (chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine), or a combination of both. Other reported treatments include **iron chelators** and oral **cholestyramine**.

### <mark>Phlebotomy</mark>
<mark>Phlebotomy remains the **treatment of choice** for PCT.</mark> <mark>Numerous studies have demonstrated its safety and efficacy, first introduced by Ippen.</mark> <mark>It works by depleting excessive hepatic iron stores, a hallmark of PCT.</mark> <mark>Biochemical remission has been achieved in patients both with and without overt iron overload.</mark> <mark>Replenishment of iron after remission has led to recurrence of both biochemical and clinical disease activity.</mark> Abstinence from environmental triggers—particularly alcohol—may induce remission, though this process can take months to years.

The therapeutic efficacy of phlebotomy may be attributed to several mechanisms:

1. **Iron effects on ALA synthase**: Iron enhances the induction of **ALA synthase** in response to drugs and hepatic porphyrinogenic stimuli (e.g., hexachlorobenzene). Depleting iron reduces the inducibility of ALA synthase, thereby decreasing hepatic porphyrin production.

2. **Iron depletion effects on other heme pathway enzymes**: Ferrous iron inhibits **uroporphyrinogen (UROGEN) decarboxylase** and increases the rate of hepatic porphyrin synthesis from ALA or PBG. Iron removal may restore UROGEN decarboxylase activity and reduce excessive porphyrinogenesis. This mechanism has been supported by studies in genetically engineered mice.

# NON-ACUTE AND ACUTE PORPHYRIAS

<mark>Patients with all forms of non-acute porphyria manifest cutaneous findings predominantly on sun-exposed body areas.</mark> <mark>The non-acute porphyrias include **porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT)**, the most prevalent type of porphyria overall; **erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP)**; **congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP)**; and **hepatoerythropoietic porphyria (HEP)**, the homozygous variant of PCT.</mark> <mark>These disorders are characterized by variable cutaneous features, including mild to severe photosensitivity, increased skin fragility, vesicles and bullae, burning and stinging sensations, edema, pruritus, hypertrichosis, scarring, hyperpigmentation, and mild to severe scleroderma-like changes.</mark>

The acute porphyrias include **acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)**, **variegate porphyria (VP)**, **hereditary coproporphyria (HCP)**, and **ALA dehydratase deficiency porphyria (plumboporphyria)**. AIP is the most common acute porphyria worldwide, although VP predominates in certain regions such as Chile and South Africa. Acute porphyrias are primarily associated with neurovisceral symptoms, including episodic abdominal pain, which can be mistaken for surgical emergencies such as acute appendicitis or diverticulitis. Treatment with analgesics may prolong or worsen the attack in some cases.

In addition to neurovisceral manifestations, patients with VP and HCP may also develop cutaneous symptoms—such as photosensitivity, skin fragility, bullous lesions on sun-exposed areas, erosions, scarring, and pigmentary changes—due to accumulation of photosensitizing porphyrins. Therefore, VP and HCP are classified as **neurocutaneous porphyrias**, distinguishing them from AIP and ALA dehydratase deficiency porphyria, which do not involve cutaneous abnormalities.

Acute attacks can be precipitated by various factors, including certain drugs (e.g., barbiturates) and general anesthesia. A particularly serious complication is **muscle weakness**, which may range from mild involvement of small muscle groups to flaccid paralysis affecting multiple limbs, leading to paraplegia and respiratory compromise. This can be accompanied by severe sensory loss and amyotrophy. In some cases, paralysis progresses rapidly and may involve cranial nerves or resemble Guillain-Barré syndrome.

Ethanol and estrogens are known triggers of acute attacks in AIP, VP, and HCP. These agents can also exacerbate PCT, although acute neurovisceral attacks do not occur in PCT, and the underlying mechanisms are likely different.

# Pathophysiology of Cutaneous Signs and Symptoms in the Non-Acute Porphyrias

<mark>Photosensitivity is the hallmark cutaneous manifestation in non-acute porphyrias.</mark> <mark>It occurs in PCT, EPP, CEP, HEP, and also in VP and HCP—disorders in which both cutaneous and neurovisceral symptoms may be present.</mark> <mark>The essential factor underlying photosensitivity is elevated levels of **plasma and tissue porphyrins**, which act as potent photosensitizers due to their unique photobiologic and spectroscopic properties.</mark>

<mark>In contrast, patients with AIP or ALA dehydratase deficiency porphyria accumulate **aminolevulinic acid (ALA)** and **porphobilinogen (PBG)**—non-photosensitizing precursors—and therefore do not develop photosensitivity.</mark>

Patients with erythropoietic porphyrias, particularly EPP, often report intense burning pain and pruritus during or after sunlight exposure. A "priming" effect has been described in EPP, where an initial subthreshold sun exposure appears to enhance the skin's response to subsequent exposure the following day, suggesting impaired or delayed repair of porphyrin-mediated photodamage. These painful symptoms are typically absent in chronic hepatic porphyrias like PCT and VP.

While the mechanisms of photosensitivity and sclerodermoid changes in hepatic porphyrias are partially understood, the causes of **hyperpigmentation**, **hypopigmentation**, and **hypertrichosis** remain unclear.

## Types of Porphyria Cutanea Tarda (PCT)

### <mark>Acquired (Type I) PCT</mark>
<mark>In acquired (type I) PCT, uroporphyrinogen (UROGEN) decarboxylase deficiency is restricted to the liver.</mark> <mark>This tissue-specific deficiency may result from either a liver-specific gene defect or exposure to chemicals that selectively inhibit the hepatic form of the enzyme without affecting the erythrocyte (RBC) enzyme.</mark> <mark>Certain substances trigger PCT only in susceptible individuals—such as **alcohol** and **estrogens**—while others, like **hexachlorobenzene (HCB)**, can induce the disease in nearly all exposed individuals.</mark>

### Hereditary (Type II) PCT
Hereditary (type II) PCT is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by approximately 50% reduction in UROGEN decarboxylase activity across all tissues, including RBCs and cultured skin fibroblasts. Enzyme levels show a bimodal distribution:
- A large group (>80%) has normal enzyme concentration.
- A smaller group (<20%) exhibits about half the normal amount of detectable enzyme.

Some patients with type II PCT have enzyme activity at the lower end of the normal range. Clinical penetrance is low (~20%), indicating that most individuals with the genetic defect do not develop symptoms. This implies that additional genetic or environmental factors are required for disease expression. Over 100 mutations in the *UROGEN decarboxylase* gene have been identified, many of which impair enzyme stability or cause defective pre-mRNA splicing.

### Type III PCT
Not all patients with a family history of PCT have type II disease. Some individuals have multiple affected relatives but normal RBC UROGEN decarboxylase activity. This variant has been termed **type III PCT** by some researchers. Possible explanations include:
- Inheritance of a UROGEN decarboxylase variant that appears normal immunologically but is selectively vulnerable to hepatic inhibition.
- Presence of a second inherited enzyme defect unrelated to UROGEN decarboxylase.

These hypotheses remain under investigation.

### Differential Diagnosis and Dual Porphyrias
Some cases originally classified as hereditary PCT may actually represent **variegate porphyria (VP)**, another autosomal dominant porphyria. Families with both PCT and VP have been described ("dual porphyrias"). Additionally, coexistence of PCT and **acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)** has been reported, further complicating diagnosis and classification.

## <mark>Precipitating Factors in Acquired (Type I) PCT</mark>
Multiple agents and conditions are associated with the development of sporadic (type I) PCT:

- <mark>**Alcohol**</mark>
- **Estrogenic hormones**
- **Iron overload**
- **Viral infections** (hepatitis C, HIV)
- **Polychlorinated hydrocarbons** (e.g., HCB, TCDD)
- **Hemodialysis** in renal failure

### Alcohol
Alcohol consumption is a well-established trigger for PCT. Ethanol induces hepatic **ALA synthase**, the rate-limiting enzyme in heme synthesis. It also reduces erythrocyte UROGEN decarboxylase activity in both acute and chronic alcohol use. Ethanol inhibits other heme pathway enzymes, including **ferrochelatase** and **ALA dehydratase**. Chronic alcoholism suppresses erythropoiesis and increases intestinal iron absorption, effects potentially amplified by mutations linked to **hemochromatosis**.

### Table 132-6: Drugs and Chemicals Associated with PCT
- Ethyl alcohol  
- Estrogenic hormones  
- Hexachlorobenzene (HCB)  
- Chlorinated phenols  
- Iron  
- 2,3,7,8-Tetrachlorodibenzo-*p*-dioxin (TCDD)  
- Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs)  
- Herbicides: 2,4-dichloro- and 2,4,5-trichlorophenoxyacetic acid

## <mark>Wet Beriberi and Thiamine Deficiency</mark>

<mark>A red, burning tongue and peripheral edema have also been observed with wet beriberi.</mark>

### <mark>Laboratory Testing</mark>

Diagnosis of thiamine deficiency is made by measurement of erythrocyte thiamine transketolase activity or blood thiamine concentration. <mark>The more reliable measure is erythrocyte thiamine transketolase activity before and after thiamine pyrophosphate stimulation, expressed as the percentage of thiamine pyrophosphate effect.</mark> <mark>Normal values are up to 15 percent.</mark>

### Treatment

Thiamine is a cofactor in multiple metabolic pathways, so daily requirements are based on caloric intake, with current recommendations of 0.5 mg per 1000 kcal.

Treatment can be administered intravenously, intramuscularly, or orally. For beriberi, treatment is typically initiated with intravenous or intramuscular thiamine at 50 to 100 mg per day for 7 to 14 days, followed by oral supplementation until full recovery is achieved.

---

## <mark>Vitamin B₂ (Riboflavin)</mark>

### <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>

Riboflavin was first identified in 1879 as a fluorescent yellow-green compound in milk. <mark>It functions in two coenzymes: flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and flavin-adenine dinucleotide (FAD), which play key roles in oxidation-reduction reactions during cellular respiration and oxidative phosphorylation.</mark> <mark>These coenzymes are also involved in vitamin B₆ (pyridoxine) metabolism.</mark>

Recent studies suggest riboflavin deficiency may contribute to elevated plasma homocysteine levels, impaired iron metabolism, and night blindness.

Dietary sources include dairy products, nuts, meat, eggs, whole grains, enriched breads, fatty fish, and green leafy vegetables. Most dietary riboflavin is present as FAD or FMN, which are hydrolyzed to free riboflavin by brush border enzymes in the small intestine. Free riboflavin is then absorbed via active transport in the proximal small bowel.

Deficiency can result from:

- Inadequate intake
- <mark>Malabsorption</mark>
- Phototherapy

At-risk populations include alcoholics, the elderly, and adolescents due to poor nutrition. Riboflavin deficiency is endemic in parts of India, China, and Iran where diets rely heavily on unenriched cereals.

Infants of riboflavin-deficient mothers are at risk because breast milk levels reflect maternal status. After weaning, deficiency risk increases if alternative sources like milk are not introduced. Protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) exacerbates deficiency by impairing the kidney’s ability to conserve riboflavin.

Phototherapy for neonatal jaundice causes photodegradation of riboflavin. Certain drugs also interfere with riboflavin metabolism:

- **Chlorpromazine** and tricyclic antidepressants inhibit gastrointestinal absorption.
- **Borate** displaces riboflavin from binding sites, increases urinary excretion, and inhibits riboflavin-dependent enzymes.

### <mark>Clinical Findings</mark>

Acute riboflavin deficiency presents with deep red erythema, epidermal necrolysis, and mucositis. Symptom severity correlates with the degree of deficiency.

<mark>Chronic deficiency, or **ariboflavinosis**, develops 3 to 5 months after inadequate intake.</mark> <mark>Skin and mucous membrane changes are predominant.</mark>

- <mark>**Angular stomatitis**: Begins as small papules at the mouth corners, progressing to ulcers and macerated, bleeding fissures that extend laterally.</mark>
- <mark>**Cheilosis**: Marked by erythema, dryness (xerosis), and vertical fissuring of the lips.</mark>
- <mark>**Glossitis**: Early stage shows prominent lingual papillae; as deficiency progresses, papillae atrophy, resulting in a smooth, swollen, magenta-colored tongue.</mark>

## <mark>VITAMIN B₆ (PYRIDOXINE)</mark>

### <mark>Etiology and Pathogenesis</mark>  
<mark>Vitamin B₆ refers to three interconvertible forms: **pyridoxine**, **pyridoxamine**, and **pyridoxal**.</mark> Humans cannot synthesize these compounds and must obtain them from the diet. Rich sources include meats, whole grains, vegetables, and nuts. Food processing can reduce the bioavailability of vitamin B₆, which is absorbed via passive diffusion in the jejunum. <mark>The primary active form is **pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP)**.</mark>

Vitamin B₆ serves as a coenzyme in numerous metabolic pathways, including:
- Amino acid **decarboxylation** and **transamination**
- **Gluconeogenesis**
- Conversion of **tryptophan to niacin**
- **Sphingolipid**, **prostaglandin**, and **neurotransmitter synthesis**

Because of its role in tryptophan-to-niacin conversion, clinical features of vitamin B₆ deficiency may resemble those of **niacin deficiency (pellagra)**.

### Epidemiology  
Dietary deficiency is rare due to widespread availability of vitamin B₆ in foods. However, deficiency can occur in:
- **Alcoholics** (due to poor nutrition)
- Patients with **malabsorption syndromes** (e.g., Crohn disease, celiac disease)
- Individuals taking certain **medications**:
  - **Isoniazid**, **hydralazine**, **penicillamine**: bind to pyridoxal-5-phosphate, increasing excretion and reducing coenzyme activity
  - **Oral contraceptives**: may increase demand or reduce levels

### Clinical Findings  
<mark>Deficiency manifests with dermatologic, mucosal, neurologic, and systemic symptoms:</mark>

#### <mark>Dermatologic and Mucosal Features:</mark>
- <mark>**Seborrheic-like dermatitis** affecting the face, scalp, neck, shoulders, buttocks, and perineum</mark>
- <mark>**Photodermatitis**</mark>
- <mark>**Glossitis**: red, painful, ulcerated tongue with flattening of filiform papillae</mark>
- <mark>**Cheilitis** and **angular stomatitis (cheilosis)**</mark>
- <mark>**Conjunctivitis**</mark>

<mark>These findings constitute an **oculo-orogenital syndrome** similar to that seen in **riboflavin deficiency**.</mark>

#### Neurologic and Systemic Symptoms:
- **Peripheral neuropathy**, paresthesias, weakness
- **Confusion**, depression, irritability
- **Nausea, vomiting, anorexia**
- **Anemia** (due to impaired heme synthesis)

The clinical picture often mimics **pellagra** because vitamin B₆ is essential for converting tryptophan into niacin.

#### Toxicity:
Excessive intake of vitamin B₆ (usually from supplements) can cause **sensory peripheral neuropathy**, but typically does **not produce skin findings**.

### Laboratory Testing  
- **Plasma pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP)** is the standard test for assessing vitamin B₆ status.
- **Low PLP levels** confirm deficiency.

### Treatment  
- **Recommended daily intake**:
  - Adult males: 2 mg/day
  - Adult females: 1.6 mg/day
  - Infants: ~0.3 mg/day
- **Therapeutic dose**: 100 mg pyridoxine daily
- Discontinue offending medications if possible

**Response to therapy**:
- Oral lesions resolve within **days**
- Skin and hematologic abnormalities improve within **weeks**
- Neurologic symptoms may take **months** to resolve

---

## VITAMIN B₉ (FOLATE)

### Etiology and Pathogenesis  
Folate is abundant in many foods, especially:
- Liver
- Wheat bran and other grains
- Leafy green vegetables
- Dried beans

The active form, **tetrahydrofolate (THF)**, functions as a coenzyme in **single-carbon transfer reactions**, critical for:
- Amino acid metabolism
- Purine and pyrimidine synthesis (essential for DNA replication)

#### Causes of Deficiency:
- **Malabsorption**:
  - Celiac disease
  - Chronic diarrhea
  - Post-gastrectomy state
- **Increased demand**:
  - Pregnancy
  - Hemolytic anemias
  - Rapid cell turnover
- **Antifolate medications**:
  - **Methotrexate**
  - **Trimethoprim**
  - **Pyrimethamine**
  - **Oral contraceptives** (mild effect)

These agents interfere with folate metabolism or absorption, leading to functional deficiency.

# <mark>CLINICAL FINDINGS</mark>

A consensus development conference was held by the National Institutes of Health in 1987 to establish diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1), with the goal of improving clinical research and patient care. The conference identified seven diagnostic features (Table 142-1), and it was recommended that two or more of these criteria be present to establish a diagnosis of NF-1. These criteria have proven highly effective and remain in use without modification more than 20 years later.

## <mark>Café-au-Lait Spots</mark>

<mark>Café-au-lait spots are flat, pigmented macules and are often the first clinical manifestation of NF-1 (Fig.</mark> 142-1). <mark>They are frequently present at birth and tend to increase in number during infancy and early childhood, with new spots commonly appearing throughout the first decade of life.</mark> <mark>As the child grows, existing spots also enlarge proportionally.</mark> <mark>Although they can occur anywhere on the body, they are rarely found on the face.</mark> <mark>The size, shape, and borders of café-au-lait spots are not diagnostically predictive; however, most spots in NF-1 are oval with smooth, well-defined margins.</mark>

<mark>The commonly cited notion that smooth-edged café-au-lait spots suggest NF-1 while irregular borders are more typical of McCune-Albright syndrome can be misleading and should be interpreted cautiously (Box 142-1).</mark> <mark>When café-au-lait spots overlap, the area of overlap may appear darker than either individual spot.</mark> <mark>When located within mongolian spots, they are often surrounded by a lighter pigmented halo.</mark>

<mark>The number or distribution of café-au-lait spots does not correlate with disease severity in NF-1.</mark> <mark>Additionally, the location of these macules does not predict where neurofibromas will develop.</mark>

<mark>Histologically, café-au-lait spots consist of clusters of heavily pigmented melanocytes of neural crest origin in the epidermis.</mark> <mark>These cells may contain increased numbers of "giant" melanosomes or melanin macroglobules, but these findings are not specific to NF-1 and have no diagnostic utility in biopsy specimens.</mark>

### TABLE 142-1 Diagnostic Criteria for Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF-1)<sup>a</sup>

- <mark>Six or more café-au-lait macules >5 mm in greatest diameter in prepubertal individuals or >15 mm in postpubertal individuals</mark>  
- <mark>Two or more neurofibromas of any type, or one plexiform neurofibroma</mark>  
- <mark>Freckling in the axillary or inguinal regions</mark>  
- <mark>Optic pathway glioma</mark>  
- <mark>Two or more iris Lisch nodules</mark>  
- <mark>A distinctive osseous lesion, such as sphenoid dysplasia or thinning of the long bone cortex, with or without pseudarthrosis</mark>  
- <mark>A first-degree relative (parent, sibling, or offspring) with NF-1 by the above criteria</mark>  

<mark><sup>a</sup> Two or more criteria required for diagnosis.</mark>

### <mark>Box 142-1</mark>  
**Differential Diagnosis of Syndromes Associated with Multiple Café-au-Lait Spots<sup>a</sup>**

- Neurofibromatosis type 1  
- Familial café-au-lait spots  
- LEOPARD syndrome (multiple lentigines, electrocardiographic abnormalities, ocular hypertelorism, pulmonary stenosis, abnormalities of the genitalia, growth retardation, deafness)  
- Neurofibromatosis type 2  
- McCune-Albright syndrome (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia)  
- Tuberous sclerosis  
- Fanconi anemia  
- Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B  
- Bannayan-Riley-Ruvalcaba syndrome  
- Bloom syndrome  
- Ataxia-telangiectasia  

<sup>a</sup> Listed in approximate order of typical number of café-au-lait macules.

# <mark>Café-au-Lait Spots</mark>

<mark>Café-au-lait spots may appear darker when overlapping due to increased pigment concentration.</mark> <mark>When present within Mongolian spots, they are typically surrounded by a lighter pigmented halo.</mark> The number of café-au-lait spots does not correlate with disease severity in neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1), and their location does not predict where neurofibromas will develop.

<mark>These macules represent clusters of heavily pigmented melanocytes of neural crest origin in the epidermis.</mark> While the melanocytes may contain increased numbers of "giant" melanosomes or melanin macroglobules, these features are not unique to NF-1 and have no diagnostic value in biopsy specimens.

<mark>The diagnostic criterion for NF-1 is the presence of six or more café-au-lait spots greater than 5 mm in diameter in prepubertal individuals or greater than 1.5 cm in adults.</mark> Among children eventually diagnosed with NF-1, 53% have six or more such spots by age 3 years, and 97% by age 6 years. Light brown macules resembling café-au-lait spots can also occur in red-headed children, particularly of Irish descent; however, these children usually have fewer than six macules and lack other signs of NF-1. Additionally, infants with multiple lentiginosis syndrome or LEOPARD syndrome (characterized by multiple lentigines, electrocardiographic abnormalities, ocular hypertelorism, pulmonary stenosis, genital abnormalities, growth retardation, and deafness) may present with café-au-lait macules at birth or during infancy, with lentigines appearing later in childhood.

# Intertriginous Freckling

<mark>Small café-au-lait spots less than 5 mm in diameter are termed freckles and commonly appear in the axillae, inguinal regions, and beneath the breasts.</mark> <mark>Unlike common sun-induced freckles, these lesions are not related to UV exposure and are considered virtually pathognomonic of NF-1 (Crowe sign).</mark> <mark>By age 6 years, 81% of children ultimately diagnosed with NF-1 will exhibit intertriginous freckling.</mark>

# Discrete Neurofibromas (See also Chap. 127)

Neurofibromas are benign nerve sheath tumors composed of Schwann cells, mast cells, fibroblasts, and perineural cells. They arise from peripheral nerves and present as discrete masses. Cutaneous neurofibromas protrude slightly above the skin surface or lie just beneath it, often with an overlying violaceous discoloration. They are softer than surrounding tissue and may produce a "buttonholing" sensation when palpated (Fig. 142-3). 

Subcutaneous neurofibromas, which develop under the skin or deep in visceral tissues, are generally firmer. Those originating from dorsal root ganglia can extend through neural foramina, compressing the spinal cord and forming a "dumbbell" shape. Cervical subcutaneous neurofibromas may feel like a "beaded necklace" and are frequently mistaken for lymphadenopathy. Fewer than 20% of children under 10 years of age develop cutaneous neurofibromas.

# THE NEUROFIBROMATOSES

# AT A GLANCE

<mark>Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF-1), an autosomal dominant condition, occurs at an incidence of 1 in 3000 live births.</mark> <mark>Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF-2), a separate autosomal dominant disorder, occurs at an incidence of 1 in 40,000 live births.</mark>

<mark>NF-1 can be diagnosed clinically if two of the following features are present:</mark>  
- <mark>Six or more café-au-lait spots (larger than 0.5 cm in children, larger than 1.5 cm in adults)</mark>  
- <mark>Intertriginous freckling</mark>  
- <mark>Two or more cutaneous neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma</mark>  
- <mark>Optic nerve glioma</mark>  
- <mark>Characteristic bony lesion</mark>  
- <mark>Iris Lisch nodules</mark>  
- <mark>A first-degree relative with NF-1</mark>  

<mark>Cutaneous neurofibromas are softer than the surrounding connective tissue and protrude just above the skin surface or lie just under the skin.</mark> <mark>Subcutaneous neurofibromas, which arise from peripheral nerves and can be located under the skin or deep in the viscera, are generally much harder.</mark>

<mark>Plexiform neurofibromas, typically present at birth or evident within the first few years of life, may cause disfigurement, blindness (due to amblyopia, glaucoma, or proptosis), loss of limb function, or organ dysfunction through compression of vital structures.</mark> <mark>These individuals appear to have an increased risk of facial dysmorphism, mental retardation, early appearance of neurofibromas, and the presence of plexiform neurofibromas.</mark> <mark>There is evidence that NF-1 is more severe when inherited from the mother rather than the father.</mark>

<mark>The hallmark of NF-2 is the presence of bilateral vestibular schwannomas.</mark> <mark>Individuals with NF-2 are also at increased risk for developing multiple meningiomas, schwannomas, gliomas, and neurofibromas throughout the neural axis.</mark>

<mark>Segmental NF-1 involves manifestations of NF-1—typically café-au-lait macules and neurofibromas—limited to one region of the body.</mark> <mark>This results from a post-zygotic mutation in the *NF1* gene, leading to somatic mosaicism.</mark>

# Molecular Biology

The *NF1* gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 17 and encodes a protein called **neurofibromin**. Homozygosity for mutant *NF1* alleles has not been reported, likely because it is a lethal condition.

*NF1* has an unusually high mutation rate, estimated at $2.4$ to $10 \times 10^{-5}$ gametes per generation—one of the highest rates among known inherited disorders. This may be due to the large size of the gene, which spans $350\ \text{kb}$ of genomic DNA and contains 59 exons encoding a protein of over 2800 amino acids. Alternatively, the gene may have structural features that make it particularly prone to mutation.

New mutations account for approximately 50% of NF-1 cases and occur most frequently on the paternally inherited allele. Unlike many other autosomal dominant disorders, the frequency of new mutations does not increase with advancing paternal age.

Most *NF1* mutations lead to reduced intracellular levels of neurofibromin, which is sufficient to cause the clinical features of the disease. Tumorigenesis—such as the development of benign dermal neurofibromas—requires inactivation of the normal *NF1* allele in somatic cells, a process known as **loss of heterozygosity**. This two-hit mechanism is characteristic of **tumor suppressor genes**, as seen in other inherited cancer predisposition syndromes like retinoblastoma and Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Tumor formation occurs when both copies of the gene are inactivated: the first by an inherited mutation, the second by a somatic mutation.

# POSITION STATEMENT

## <mark>Position statement: LEPROSY: Diagnosis, treatment and follow-up</mark>

### Abstract

Background: Leprosy, or Hansen's disease, is a chronic infection caused by *Mycobacterium leprae* (M. leprae) or *Mycobacterium lepromatosis* (M. lepromatosis). In Europe, most leprosy cases are imported, although occasional cases arise from old endemic foci. The disease is often not suspected due to its diminished emphasis in medical education. In the late 20th century, global health priorities shifted toward tuberculosis and HIV, leading to a reduction in the WHO leprosy programme under the assumption that leprosy was nearly eliminated. This lack of awareness contributes to harmful diagnostic delays.

### Introduction

Leprosy, also known as Hansen’s disease, is a chronic infection caused by *Mycobacterium leprae* or *Mycobacterium lepromatosis*. While most cases in Europe are imported, sporadic cases continue to emerge from historical endemic areas. The condition is frequently overlooked because it is no longer a focus in medical training. During the late twentieth century, attention shifted to tuberculosis (TB) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), resulting in a scaling down of the WHO leprosy programme based on the belief that leprosy had been largely eradicated.

In 2005, the WHO declared leprosy eliminated as a public health problem globally. However, this declaration was premature. To date, approximately 250,000 new cases are reported annually worldwide, with stable incidence and prevalence rates. With increasing migration from endemic regions, the risk of leprosy in Europe is rising. Current immigrant populations often live in overcrowded and suboptimal conditions—factors that may facilitate transmission, unlike earlier migration patterns.

Patients are now being diagnosed across the Western world, often after significant diagnostic delays, leading to lifelong disabilities. Medical curricula provide minimal coverage of leprosy, leaving even specialists such as dermatologists, neurologists, and rheumatologists poorly equipped to recognize it. Lack of awareness remains a primary reason for missed diagnoses. This position statement aims to improve physician awareness and understanding of leprosy in the European context.

### Diagnosis

Leprosy primarily affects the peripheral nerves, skin, and mucosa—especially the upper respiratory tract. Skin lesions are typically the first noticeable sign, contributing to its classification as a dermatological condition. If untreated, leprosy can lead to permanent damage to the skin, nerves, limbs, and eyes. Tissue damage results partly from direct *M. leprae* infiltration, but the majority of pathology arises from immunological reactions.

Secondary infections due to trauma—following sensory loss—can lead to tissue destruction. Bone and cartilage resorption may occur, resulting in shortening and deformities of fingers, toes, and the nose (clinical features illustrated in deformed hands due to nerve damage and secondary infection).

Patients may report:
- Loss of sensation in skin lesions, hands, or feet
- Aches and pains in the face or limbs
- Numbness, "sleepy" or "dead" feelings
- Paresthesias described as "ants running under the skin" in affected areas

Skin lesions typically present as hypopigmented or erythematous macules, papules, nodules, or plaques, which may be skin-colored or slightly red.

Clinically, leprosy is diagnosed when a patient exhibits at least two of the three cardinal signs. However, in endemic areas, the WHO considers the presence of a single cardinal sign sufficient for diagnosis—though this approach sometimes overlooks nerve enlargement.

The three well-established cardinal signs of leprosy (recognized for over 100 years) are:

1. **Loss of sensation in a skin lesion**  
2. **Enlarged peripheral nerve**  
3. **Positive skin smears**

Currently, there are no specific laboratory tests to confirm leprosy. Available tests support classification, monitoring, and detection of relapse but are not diagnostic on their own.

Sensory loss is assessed using a wisp of cotton wool. The test involves gentle touch (not brushing) of the lesion and surrounding skin to evaluate perception.

## <mark>Classification and Clinical Forms of Leprosy</mark>

<mark>Leprosy may resolve spontaneously (in many cases) or progress into one of the clinical types described in the **Ridley-Jopling classification**, depending on the development of cell-mediated immunity (CMI).</mark> Another challenging group is **pure neural leprosy**, characterized by nerve involvement without skin lesions. Its reported frequency ranges from 1 to 10%, varying by geographic region and level of clinical awareness.

For field use, the **World Health Organization (WHO)** simplifies classification based on the number of skin lesions:
- <mark>**Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy**: Five or fewer skin lesions.</mark>
- **Multibacillary (MB) leprosy**: More than five skin lesions.

While this system is practical, studies indicate that up to 30% of patients may be misclassified as PB using this method alone, leading to potential undertreatment.

---

## Treatment

The earliest documented treatment with modest efficacy was **chaulmoogra oil**, referenced in the *Sushruta Samhita* (600 BC). Though effects were limited, some benefit was observed in paucibacillary cases.

<mark>The first effective antimicrobial therapy emerged in 1943 with **promin**, an intravenous sulfone.</mark> <mark>This was soon followed by the introduction of **dapsone (diaminodiphenylsulfone, DDS)**, an oral sulfone that became the standard of care.</mark> <mark>However, by the 1970s, **dapsone resistance** became widespread.</mark> <mark>With the availability of **rifampicin (RMP)**, combination therapy was advocated to prevent resistance.</mark>

<mark>In 1982, the **WHO Chemotherapy Study Group** formally recommended multidrug therapy (MDT), combining **rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine**, depending on classification.</mark>

<mark>Today, **WHO-recommended multidrug therapy (MDT)** remains the global standard and is widely implemented.</mark>

---

## Multidrug Therapy (MDT) Regimens

### Paucibacillary Leprosy (PB)
- <mark>**Rifampicin**: 600 mg, once monthly under supervision for 6 months.</mark>
- <mark>**Dapsone**: 100 mg daily, unsupervised.</mark>

<mark>For a 60 kg adult, treatment can be discontinued after **6 supervised monthly doses administered within 9 months**.</mark>

A recent proposal suggests adding **clofazimine (Lamprene)** to the 6-month PB regimen to reduce undertreatment and harmonize therapy across classifications. This approach aims to minimize reliance on clinical classification, though it remains under debate among clinicians.

---

### Multibacillary Leprosy (MB)
- <mark>**Monthly (supervised)**: 600 mg rifampicin + 300 mg clofazimine (Lamprene).</mark>
- <mark>**Daily (unsupervised)**: 100 mg dapsone + 50 mg clofazimine.</mark>

<mark>The official WHO recommendation is **12 supervised monthly doses within 18 months**.</mark> However, many clinicians modify this:
- **Low bacterial index (BI)**: 12 monthly doses over 18 months.
- **High bacterial index (BI ≥ 4)**: 24 monthly doses over 36 months.

Doses are standardized for a 60 kg patient.

---

## Uniform MDT (U-MDT)

The WHO is currently evaluating **Uniform MDT (U-MDT)** — a **6-month regimen using rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine for all leprosy patients**, regardless of classification. This approach eliminates the need for classification.

However, this proposal is **controversial** and faces strong opposition from many clinicians due to concerns about undertreating multibacillary cases.

---

## Treatment Outcomes and Safety Considerations

- The established MDT regimens have proven highly effective, with **relapse rates below 4%**.
- However, **follow-up duration for MB leprosy is often insufficient**, raising concerns about late relapses.
- **Dapsone-related haemolysis** is a known risk, particularly in **Nordic Caucasians**, even in the absence of G6PD deficiency. Reducing the dose to **50 mg daily** maintains efficacy while significantly reducing anaemia, likely due to genetic factors.
- <mark>**Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome** is more common in **Nepalese and Chinese patients**, requiring heightened clinical vigilance.</mark>

# <mark>CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS</mark>

## <mark>Presentation</mark>

The presence of any friable, non-healing lesion should raise the suspicion of skin cancer. <mark>Frequently, basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is diagnosed in patients who report that the lesion bled briefly, then healed completely, only to recur later.</mark> BCC typically develops on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck but can occur anywhere on the body. Common features include translucency, ulceration, telangiectasias, and a rolled border. Clinical characteristics vary among sub-types, which include nodular, superficial, morpheaform (sclerosing), pigmented BCC, and fibroepithelioma of Pinkus (FEP).

## Basal Cell Carcinoma Sub-Types

### Nodular Basal Cell Carcinoma

Nodular BCC is the most common clinical sub-type (Fig. 115-1). It typically occurs on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck and presents as a translucent papule or nodule, depending on duration. Telangiectasias are commonly present, and the lesion often has a rolled border. Larger lesions with central necrosis are historically referred to as rodent ulcers (Fig. 115-2). The differential diagnosis includes traumatized dermal nevus and amelanotic melanoma.

### Pigmented Basal Cell Carcinoma

Pigmented BCC is a variant of nodular BCC characterized by increased melanization. It appears as a hyperpigmented, translucent papule and may be eroded (Fig. 115-3). The differential diagnosis primarily includes nodular melanoma.

### Superficial Basal Cell Carcinoma

Superficial BCC most commonly occurs on the trunk and presents as an erythematous, well-demarcated patch that may resemble eczema (Fig. 115-4). An isolated patch of "eczema" that fails to respond to topical treatment should prompt suspicion for superficial BCC.

### Morpheaform (Sclerosing) Basal Cell Carcinoma

Morpheaform BCC is an aggressive variant with distinct clinical and histologic features. Lesions often have an ivory-white appearance and may resemble a scar or a small, indurated plaque (Fig. 115-5). This sub-type is more infiltrative and has a higher risk of recurrence.

# <mark>Superficial Basal Cell Carcinoma</mark>

<mark>Superficial basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is characterized microscopically by buds of malignant basaloid cells extending from the basal layer of the epidermis into the upper dermis.</mark> <mark>The peripheral cells typically show palisading.</mark> <mark>Epidermal atrophy may be present, and dermal invasion is usually minimal.</mark> This subtype is most commonly found on the trunk and extremities, although it can also occur on the head and neck. <mark>A chronic inflammatory infiltrate is often present in the upper dermis.</mark>

# Morpheaform Basal Cell Carcinoma

<mark>Morpheaform (or infiltrative) BCC consists of thin strands or cords of tumor cells embedded within a dense fibrous stroma.</mark> <mark>The tumor cells are closely packed and may be as narrow as a single cell in thickness.</mark> <mark>These strands extend deeply into the dermis, often beyond the clinically apparent margins, making the tumor larger than it appears on physical examination.</mark> Recurrent BCCs may also exhibit similar infiltrative patterns within scar tissue.

# Fibroepithelioma of Pinkus

<mark>Fibroepithelioma of Pinkus (FEP) is a variant of BCC that presents histologically as long, interwoven strands of basaloid cells within a fibrous stroma.</mark> It shares features with both reticulated seborrheic keratoses and superficial BCC, making diagnosis dependent on careful histologic evaluation.

# Differential Diagnosis

## Nodular BCC
- Dermal nevus  
- Squamous cell carcinoma  
- Appendageal tumor  
- Dermatofibroma  
- Scar  
- Seborrheic keratosis  

## Pigmented BCC
- Nodular melanoma  
- Superficial spreading melanoma  
- Lentigo maligna melanoma  
- Appendageal tumor  
- Compound nevus  
- Blue nevus  

## <mark>Superficial BCC</mark>
- Bowen disease  
- Mammary or extramammary Paget disease  
- Superficial spreading melanoma  
- Single plaque of psoriasis  
- Single plaque of eczema  

## Morpheaform BCC
- Scar  
- Morphea  
- Trichoepithelioma  

## Fibroepithelioma of Pinkus
- Skin tag  
- Papillomatous dermal nevus  
- Fibroma  

# Treatment

Management of BCC depends on anatomic location, tumor subtype, and histologic features. Treatment options include Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS), standard surgical excision, destructive modalities (e.g., curettage and desiccation, cryotherapy), radiotherapy, and topical chemotherapy.

The best chance for cure is with appropriate initial treatment of primary BCC, as recurrent tumors are more likely to recur again and cause extensive local tissue destruction. An algorithmic approach to management should be followed based on risk stratification.

## Mohs Micrographic Surgery (See Chap. 245)

Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) provides superior margin control compared to standard excision, allowing for maximal tissue preservation while achieving high cure rates. Studies report a recurrence rate of **1%** for primary BCCs treated with MMS, significantly lower than other modalities:
- Standard excision: 10%  
- Curettage and desiccation (C&D): 7.7%  
- Radiotherapy (XRT): 8.7%  
- Cryotherapy: 7.5%  

For recurrent BCCs, MMS has a recurrence rate of **5.6%**, again outperforming:
- Excision: 17.6%  
- XRT: 9.8%  
- C&D: 40%  

MMS is the treatment of choice for morpheaform BCC, poorly demarcated tumors, incompletely excised lesions, and other high-risk cases.
